title: Old Dams Come Down, and Fish Swim Back
summary:
In the northeastern United States, people are taking down old dams. Now fish called river herring are coming back.

A dam is a wall that blocks a river. Dams can store water or make electricity. But they can also stop fish from swimming upstream to lay their eggs.

Long ago, people in the East built many dams to power mills. By the mid-1800s, there were more than 65,000 mills. Scientists say these dams cost New England nearly 20 billion pounds of alewives, a kind of river herring.

Since 1912, more than 2,300 dams have been removed in the US. In 2024, Pennsylvania alone removed 27 old dams. Still, at least 35,000 dams block fish in the Northeast.

The results can be big. In 2025, about six million river herring returned to Maine's Penobscot River. That was double the number from two years before.

Fish biologist Nathan Furey's team puts tiny tags, about the size of a grain of rice, in fish to count how many make it upstream.
why_it_matters: Rivers near your home could fill with fish again when old barriers are removed.
